doc.title: Billy Bauer interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, March 22, 1998

title: Small group with Chubby Jackson and Lennie Tristano
summary: A short-lived group clashed: Lennie wanted him not to play rhythm while Chubby pushed ahead, with Arnold Fishkin on bass.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: You played for a while in a smaller group with Chubby and Lennie Tristano?

No, well see Chubby is a different type of player. He did that kind of playing. Lennie was, I don’t know if you want to say sophisticated or what. But we played a couple of jobs together but really Arnold Fishkin, Chubby was supposed to come in — I thought Chubby would be with Lennie and myself and Chubby. Because Chubby operated this see. But he put Arnold Friskin with us, the bass player. But a couple of dates Chubby was angling around. One of them was on 52nd Street. And I was playing like I was playing with Lennie because Lennie didn’t want me to play rhythm. He wanted me to do anything but don’t play rhythm. You get with Chubby and Chubby going “come on!” Because he was looking to get somewhere, and Lennie would be laying back. Oh that was a miserable couple of nights. See they just—

Yeah, they are two different schools. Well Lennie always used to have trouble most of the time with drummers, because they would fill in. They were used to sort of bebop you know. And he didn’t want them because they destroyed, well now I realize he could be playing other three beat or five beat phrases, and they’d put it in where they thought it should be and so he’d generally tell them just play time. See and Chubby was like that too with the bass. Well they didn’t — not that they hated each other or anything, it was just the two people, their playing.
